channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: Your opinion shifts to match the perceived group consensus.
item.description: A 1951 study showed that participants would give a clearly incorrect answer just to align with the rest of the group.

item.title: You selectively interpret facts to protect your existing worldview.
item.description: A 1979 study found that participants shown balanced evidence on capital punishment were convinced their original stance had been correct all along.

item.title: Your recall improves when you return to your original mood.
item.description: A 1981 study showed that participants remembered information better if they were in the same emotional state during retrieval as they were during encoding.

item.title: Your brain shuts down for half a second after focusing.
item.description: Participants show significantly reduced performance in detecting a second target when it appears 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first.

item.title: You hold losing investments far longer than winning ones.
item.description: A 1985 study found that investors are significantly more likely to sell a stock that has gained value than one that has dropped.

item.title: Random numbers influence your estimate of an unknown value.
item.description: A 1974 experiment demonstrated that participants' estimates for geopolitical statistics were significantly skewed by a random number drawn from a wheel of fortune.

item.title: You are statistically likely to choose the pre-selected option.
item.description: A 2003 study of organ donation found that countries with an opt-out policy had nearly 100% participation compared to 15% in opt-in countries.

item.title: You believe you understand how a simple zipper works.
item.description: A 2002 study showed that people consistently overestimate their grasp of complex systems until they are forced to explain them.

item.title: Your brain ignores most of an experience to save energy.
item.description: In a 1996 study, participants judged the total unpleasantness of a colonoscopy based heavily on the peak discomfort and the final moments of the procedure.

item.title: You assume you are safer than everyone else.
item.description: A 1980 study by Neil D. Weinstein published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that individuals consistently rate their own risks for negative events as lower than the risk faced by others.

item.title: You focus on one event while ignoring context.
item.description: A 2000 study showed that people overestimate the impact of a single focal event on their overall happiness.

item.title: You hold onto opinions even after being disproven.
item.description: A 1975 study showed that once an initial belief is formed, it remains influential even after the evidence supporting it is discredited.

item.title: You are a terrible judge of your future self.
item.description: A 2003 study found that people systematically underestimate how much their future preferences will change based on their current state.

item.title: You work harder as you approach a goal.
item.description: A 2006 study by Kivetz, Urminsky, and Zheng empirically resurrected the 1932 'goal-gradient hypothesis' by showing that consumers increase their purchase frequency as they approach a reward.

item.title: You feel compelled to restore your lost freedom.
item.description: Psychological reactance is a motivational state that arises when an individual's behavioral freedoms are threatened, which may lead them to resist the influence attempt to re-establish autonomy.

item.title: You overestimate how much the world focuses on you.
item.description: The spotlight effect describes your tendency to believe that your appearance and actions are more visible to others than they really are.

item.title: Your brain ignores facts that contradict your beliefs.
item.description: Motivated reasoning and biased assimilation lead people to evaluate contradictory evidence more critically than supporting evidence, causing them to perceive opposing data as less credible.

item.title: You remember events as better than they were.
item.description: The study titled 'Temporal adjustments in the evaluation of events: The rosy prospection and rosy retrospection' was published in 1997, not 1994.

item.title: The presence of others changes your moral compass.
item.description: The bystander effect demonstrates that your likelihood of intervening in an emergency decreases as the number of witnesses increases.

item.title: You change your attitude to match your behavior.
item.description: Self-perception theory suggests that when your internal beliefs are unclear, you infer them by observing your own past actions.

item.title: You create your own excuses before you even start.
item.description: Self-handicapping is the strategy of creating obstacles to performance to protect your self-esteem if you happen to fail.

item.title: Your past self is a stranger you judge harshly.
item.description: The end-of-history illusion is our tendency to believe we have reached our final personality despite significant growth over the last decade.

item.title: Small mistakes actually make you more likable.
item.description: The pratfall effect shows that highly competent people may become more appealing after a minor blunder, whereas the same mistake can make an average person appear less attractive.

item.title: You judge others by character and yourself by circumstance.
item.description: The actor-observer asymmetry explains why you interpret your own bad behavior as a situational necessity while labeling identical actions in others as personality flaws.

item.title: You avoid the unknown even when it offers rewards.
item.description: Ambiguity aversion describes the tendency to prefer options with known probabilities over options with unknown probabilities in decision-making contexts.

item.title: You notice things more frequently after learning about them.
item.description: The frequency illusion occurs when a new piece of information you recently learned suddenly seems to appear everywhere.

item.title: You perceive members of other groups as all identical.
item.description: Outgroup homogeneity is the tendency to see individuals in other groups as having fewer unique traits than people in your own group.

item.title: Your choice changes when an irrelevant option appears.
item.description: The decoy effect occurs when your preference between two choices shifts after a third, inferior option is introduced.

item.title: A minor lapse leads you to abandon all progress.
item.description: The what-the-hell effect explains why one small deviation from a goal often results in a total collapse of self-control.

item.title: The presence of others changes how you perform tasks.
item.description: Social facilitation is the tendency to improve on simple, well-learned tasks when others are watching.

item.title: You find it impossible to ignore what you already know.
item.description: The curse of knowledge causes you to overestimate how well others understand what you are explaining.

item.title: You believe you see the world objectively as it is.
item.description: Naive realism is the tendency to assume our perception of reality is the only accurate one.

item.title: You roll dice harder to influence the outcome.
item.description: People believe they have influence over random outcomes when they are personally involved in the process.

item.title: You remember the vacation better than the experience.
item.description: People report higher satisfaction for past events than they did while the events were actually occurring.

item.title: You defend your beliefs after seeing contrary data.
item.description: The 'backfire effect' refers to a proposed psychological phenomenon where contrary evidence strengthens existing beliefs, but empirical support for this effect is inconsistent and it is rarely observed in practice.

item.title: You blame the victim to feel safer yourself.
item.description: People often assume that victims of misfortune deserve their fate to maintain a belief in a just world.

item.title: You decide based on how data is phrased.
item.description: In their 1981 paper, Tversky and Kahneman demonstrated that the framing of outcomes as gains or losses influences preferences using a scenario involving 600 potential lives at risk.

item.title: You continue painful projects to avoid admitting loss.
item.description: Individuals invest more time and resources into a failing project simply because they have already invested in it.

item.title: You rewrite your own history to match current outcomes.
item.description: People consistently misremember their past predictions as being more accurate than they actually were.

item.title: You judge harmful inaction as less severe than action.
item.description: Research indicates that people rate harmful consequences resulting from inaction as more acceptable than identical harm caused by active intervention.

item.title: You believe you are more observant than you are.
item.description: A 1998 study found that a significant portion of observers failed to detect changes in a person during a real-world interaction when their attention was occupied.

item.title: You are more likely to lie for a small reward.
item.description: A 1959 study showed that people are more willing to perform a dull task for a small incentive if they convince themselves the task is actually interesting.

item.title: If it sounds familiar, you assume it is true.
item.description: A 2015 study found that statements were rated as more accurate if they had been heard previously, even when the source was labeled as unreliable.

item.title: Your ability to make sound decisions erodes throughout the day.
item.description: A 2011 study of over 1,000 judicial rulings found that parole boards were significantly more likely to grant favorable outcomes after a food break.

item.title: You judge a person's intelligence by their physical beauty.
item.description: A 1972 study found that people with attractive faces were consistently rated as having more desirable personality traits and better life prospects.

item.title: Your presence in a room matters less than you feel.
item.description: A 2000 study by Gilovich, Medvec, and Savitsky found that people suffer from the 'spotlight effect,' an egocentric bias where they overestimate the degree to which their appearance and actions are noticed by others.

item.title: You like something simply because you see it often.
item.description: A 1968 study demonstrated that conscious exposure to neutral stimuli leads to higher favorability ratings, while later studies (notably in 1980) confirmed that this effect holds even when stimuli are presented below the threshold of conscious recognition.

item.title: You prefer strangers just because they are like you.
item.description: A 1970 study found that participants assigned to arbitrary groups awarded more money to their own team, even when group members were strangers.

item.title: The silver medalist is sadder than the bronze.
item.description: A 1995 study found that Olympic silver medalists showed significantly less happiness than bronze winners.

item.title: You sabotage yourself to protect your ego.
item.description: A 1978 study found that participants chose to consume performance-inhibiting drugs when they were anxious about an upcoming test.
